title: Vitamin D
wiki_lead:
Vitamin D is a group of structurally related, fat-soluble compounds responsible for increasing intestinal absorption of calcium, along with numerous other biological functions. In humans, the most important compounds within this group are vitamin D3 (cholecalciferol) and vitamin D2 (ergocalciferol).
Unlike the other twelve vitamins, vitamin D is only conditionally essential in the diet, as with adequate skin exposure to the ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation component of sunlight there is synthesis of cholecalciferol in the deeper layers of the skin's epidermis. Vitamin D can also be obtained through diet, food fortification and dietary supplements. For most people, skin synthesis contributes more than dietary sources. Accordingly, the name "vitamin D" is arguably a misnomer, as rather than being an essential part of the diet, it acts more like a fat-soluble secosteroid hormone precursor. Nevertheless, US and other dietary guidelines generally assume that all of a person's vitamin D is taken orally, given the potential for insufficient sunlight exposure due to urban living, cultural choices for the amount of clothing worn when outdoors, and use of sunscreen because of concerns about safe sunlight exposure. In many countries, milk and plant-based milk substitutes are fortified with vitamin D3, as are breakfast cereals.
Cholecalciferol is converted in the liver to calcifediol (also known as calcidiol or 25-hydroxycholecalciferol), while ergocalciferol is converted to ercalcidiol (25-hydroxyergocalciferol). These two vitamin D metabolites, collectively referred to as 25-hydroxyvitamin D or 25(OH)D, are measured in serum to assess a person's vitamin D status. Calcifediol is further hydroxylated by the kidneys and certain immune cells to form calcitriol (1,25-dihydroxycholecalciferol; 1,25(OH)2D), the biologically active form of vitamin D. Calcitriol attaches to vitamin D receptors, which are nuclear receptors found in various tissues throughout the body. Analogous reactions occur for other vitamin D forms as well as various vitamin D analogues.
The discovery of the vitamin in 1922 was due to an effort to identify the dietary deficiency in children with rickets. Adolf Windaus received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry in 1928 for his work on the constitution of sterols and their connection with vitamins. Present day, government food fortification programs in some countries and recommendations to consume vitamin D supplements are intended to prevent or treat vitamin D deficiency, rickets, and osteomalacia. 
To date, investigators have nominally linked many other health conditions to vitamin D deficiency. However, the evidence for health benefits of vitamin D supplementation in individuals who already are vitamin D sufficient is as yet unproven.

Vitamin D is a fat-soluble secosteroid that functions as a prohormone essential for calcium and phosphorus homeostasis, primarily supporting bone health through enhanced intestinal absorption of calcium and phosphate. It exists in two main forms: vitamin D 2 (ergocalciferol), derived from plant sources and used in fortified foods and supplements, and vitamin D 3 (cholecalciferol), synthesized endogenously in the skin upon exposure to ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation from sunlight or obtained from animal-based foods like fatty fish. The primary source of vitamin D is cutaneous synthesis in the skin upon exposure to ultraviolet B (UVB) radiation from sunlight, which can produce 10,000 IU or more in 10-30 minutes of midday sun exposure depending on skin type, location, season, extent of body exposure, and other factors; this pathway accounts for the majority of vitamin D in individuals with regular sun exposure, though production is self-regulated to prevent excess. However, at higher latitudes (around 45â50Â°N) during winter months such as December, UVB radiation is typically insufficient for significant synthesis, with even prolonged exposure (several hours with large skin areas exposed) yielding little to no vitamin D, making effective production impossible or ineffective during this period. Dietary intake provides smaller amounts from natural sources such as fatty fish, fish liver oils, and UV-exposed mushrooms, fortified foods, and supplements, with vitamin D 3 generally more effective than D 2 at raising and maintaining serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels. Among natural food sources, the richest sources (approximate vitamin D content per 100 g, based on recent 2025 data) include: Cod liver oil: approximately 250 Âµg (10,000 IU) Raw cod liver: approximately 100 Âµg (4,000 IU) Herring (smoked or fresh): 22â23.5 Âµg (880â940 IU) Halibut: approximately 21 Âµg (840 IU) Salmon trout: approximately 18.7 Âµg (748 IU) Salmon: 13â20 Âµg (520â800 IU, variable according to type and preparation) Canned sardines: approximately 12â40 Âµg (variable) Other natural sources include mackerel (approximately 20 Âµg/100 g) and UV-exposed mushrooms (variable, often lower per 100 g but up to several thousand IU per serving in some treated varieties), with levels boosted significantly by sunlight or UV treatment. In contrast, common plant-based foods such as avocado, banana, kiwi, pineapple, dates, whole wheat pasta, whole wheat bread, peanut butter, rice, and other unfortified grains contain 0 Î¼g vitamin D per 100 g, as they do not naturally contain vitamin D and standard varieties are not fortified. Staple foods like grains or rice do not naturally contain significant amounts unless fortified. Natural dietary sources of vitamin D are limited. Fatty fish and fish liver oils provide the highest amounts of vitamin D3. Egg yolks contain moderate levels (around 40-50 IU per large egg, higher in pasture-raised varieties due to hen sun exposure). Beef liver provides small amounts (approximately 1 mcg or 42 IU per 3-ounce cooked serving). Unfortified dairy products like cow or goat milk are low in vitamin D (typically 20-40 IU per cup, varying with animal diet and sunlight), making them minor contributors unless fortified (often adding ~100-120 IU per cup). Fortified foods such as milk, breakfast cereals, yogurt, and orange juice are common sources. Amounts vary by preparation, source, species, fortification levels, and other factors; most diets rely on fortification and sun exposure for adequate intake. Supplements include lichen-derived Dâ as a vegan source.
Fortified orange juice is a notable vehicle for vitamin D fortification, particularly in the United States, where it became common in the early 2000s. Standard fortified orange juice typically provides approximately 100 IU (2.5 Î¼g) of vitamin D per 8-ounce (240 ml) serving, often alongside calcium. Key research has demonstrated the bioavailability of vitamin D from fortified orange juice. A 2003 study by Tangpricha et al. found that consuming orange juice fortified with 1000 IU vitamin Dâ daily for 12 weeks increased serum 25(OH)D concentrations by 150% in adults. A 2010 study by Biancuzzo et al. showed that vitamin Dâ or Dâ fortified in orange juice is as effective as oral supplements in raising and maintaining serum 25(OH)D levels, with no significant differences in bioavailability between the juice and capsule forms. This makes fortified orange juice an effective non-dairy alternative for increasing vitamin D intake, supporting bone health and potentially immune function in populations with limited sun exposure or dietary sources. In the body, vitamin D undergoes sequential metabolism: first hydroxylation in the liver to 25-hydroxyvitamin D (the main circulating form used to assess status), then further activation in the kidneys to 1,25-dihydroxyvitamin D (calcitriol), its biologically active hormone that binds to vitamin D receptors to regulate over 200 genes involved in mineral metabolism, immune modulation, and cellular differentiation. Key functions include promoting bone mineralization to prevent conditions like rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults, as well as supporting neuromuscular function, reducing inflammation, and potentially aiding in cardiovascular and immune health, though evidence for non-skeletal benefits remains mixed. The recommended dietary allowance (RDA) for adults is 15 mcg (600 IU) daily for those aged 19â70 years and 20 mcg (800 IU) for those over 70, as established by the Institute of Medicine in 2011, which updated prior guidelines and common perceptions where 400 IU was frequently regarded as adequate due to its long-standing use in preventing rickets, supplement formulations, and as the 100% Daily Value on nutrition labels until the FDA's 2016 update, with an upper limit of 100 mcg (4,000 IU) to avoid toxicity risks like hypercalcemia. Deficiency is common worldwide and is more prevalent in groups with limited sun exposure, darker skin, obesity, or malabsorption issues, leading to impaired bone health and increased fracture risk. Serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D levels below 30 nmol/L (12 ng/mL) are associated with vitamin D deficiency according to guidelines such as those from the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, while levels in the 10-19 ng/mL range are classified as mild to moderate deficiency in some clinical interpretations, potentially associated with increased risk of osteoporosis or secondary hyperparathyroidism. In contrast, many authoritative sources and clinical practices define deficiency as levels <20 ng/mL (<50 nmol/L), insufficiency as 20-29 ng/mL (50-72.5 nmol/L), and sufficiency as â¥30 ng/mL (â¥75 nmol/L), with optimal ranges often cited as 30-100 ng/mL (75-250 nmol/L). A 25-hydroxy vitamin D level of 73 ng/mL (approximately 182 nmol/L) indicates sufficient to optimal vitamin D status, well above deficiency (<20 ng/mL) and insufficiency (20-29 ng/mL) thresholds. A serum 25-hydroxyvitamin D level of 27 ng/mL is considered sufficient according to NIH guidelines, as concentrations of 20 ng/mL (50 nmol/L) or higher are adequate for most people. The 2024 Endocrine Society guideline recommends that healthy adults under 75 years of age follow the RDA (600-800 IU daily) without routine testing or additional supplementation. Decisions on supplementation should be based on individual health status and made in consultation with a healthcare professional. Conversely, excessive intake can cause vitamin D toxicity, characterized by elevated calcium levels and symptoms like nausea and kidney stones, though this is rare below the upper limit and typically associated with levels >150 ng/mL (>375 nmol/L). Ongoing research emphasizes the importance of monitoring status through blood tests, as optimal levels vary by guideline; some sources indicate 50â125 nmol/L (20â50 ng/mL) as adequate for overall health, while others suggest higher ranges such as 30-100 ng/mL for optimal function, with some guidelines noting potential adverse effects above 50 ng/mL (125 nmol/L) without clear consensus on supplementation for disease prevention beyond bone disorders.
